## My LORD,

<image-desc>Decorative square woodcut initial 'T' featuring floral patterns and a central letter T.</image-desc>

So that your Lordship may be prepared to receive what I take the liberty of presenting to you with greater openness <note>original: "Candor"</note>, I sincerely declare that it does not proceed from any prejudice. Instead, it arises from certain reasons that have firmly convinced me <note>original: "invincibly obliged"</note> that I must disagree with your Lordship’s opinion.

To prevent any suspicion that I intend to harm your Lordship’s character in this address, I have included my name—which I might otherwise have chosen to keep hidden—at the beginning of it.

Your Lordship is seen as the leader of a cause where every opponent is certain to be insulted as either a fanatical Jacobite <note>a supporter of the exiled King James II and his descendants</note>, a Catholic bigot <note>original: "Popish Bigot"</note>, or an enemy to the liberty of his country and the Protestant cause. These harsh labels are to be expected, my Lord, from a group of men who dishonor your Lordship with their excessive flattery <note>original: "Panegyricks"</note> of your work—men whose praises actually stain the character they intend to celebrate.

When Dr. *Snape* <note>Andrew Snape (1675–1742), a high-church clergyman and critic of Bishop Hoadly</note> represents your Lordship as no friend to the good order and necessary institutions of the Church, you complain about the deceptive tactics <note>original: "ill Arts"</note> of an opponent who portrays you in a false light and deliberately twists your words to increase his own *imaginary triumphs*. But, my Lord, in this regard, Dr. *Snape* only agrees with those who are considered your best friends—friends who would only remain so because they conclude that you have declared yourself against the authority of the Church. 

Does your Lordship suppose that the *T----ds*, the *H--------ks*, and the *B----ts* <note>These redacted names likely refer to radical or deist thinkers of the era, such as John Toland, whose views were considered subversive to traditional religion</note> would spend so much time and effort to justify, praise, and expand upon your Lordship’s ideas if they did not think you were committed to their cause? There is not a libertine or "freethinker" <note>original: "Loose-Thinker"</note> in *England* who does not imagine that you intend to dissolve the Church as an organized *society*, and they are ready to offer praise to your Lordship for such a supposedly worthy design. 

I do not intend to criticize your Lordship for their admiration or to implicate you in the guilt of their schemes. Rather, I want to show that an opponent does not need any malice to believe you are no friend to the constitution of the Church as a formal society, since your greatest admirers essentially proclaim this to the world in print every day through their own interpretations of your work.

After a word or two concerning a passage in your Lordship’s *Preservative* <note>Referring to Hoadly's 1716 work, *A Preservative against the Principles and Practices of the Non-jurors*</note>, I shall proceed to consider your answer to Dr. *Snape*. On page 98, you have these words: *“But when you are certain of your integrity before God, — this will lead you (as it should lead all of us) not to be afraid of the ter—”* <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the catchword "rors" indicates the next word is "terrors."</note>

...terrors of men, or the empty words of *regular* and *uninterrupted successions* <note>The doctrine of Apostolic Succession, the idea that bishops have an unbroken spiritual chain of authority stretching back to the Apostles</note>, *authoritative blessings*, *excommunications*, the *nullity* or *validity* of God’s ordinances <note>religious rituals like baptism or the Lord's Supper</note> based on *technicalities* and *trifles*, or any other such *fantasies* <note>original: "Dreams"</note>.

My Lord, this much must be implied here: do not be afraid of the terrors of men who would persuade you of the danger of being in one denomination <note>original: "Communion"</note> or another, and frighten you into specific ways of worshipping God. They would make you believe that certain sacraments and a specific clergy are necessary to recommend you to His favor. For these things, your Lordship affirms, we may disregard <note>original: "contemn"</note> if we are only certain of our own integrity.

So it follows that if a man is not a *hypocrite*, it does not matter what *religion* he belongs to. This is a proposition that seems hostile <note>original: "of an unfriendly Aspect"</note> to Christianity. But that it is entirely your Lordship’s view is plain from what you declare on page 90: *That everyone may find it true in their own conduct that their title to God’s favor cannot depend upon actually being or continuing in any particular method; but upon their real sincerity in the conduct of their conscience.* Again, on page 91: *The favor of God follows sincerity, considered as such, and consequently follows every equal degree of sincerity equally.* 

So, I hope I have not twisted <note>original: "wrested"</note> your Lordship’s meaning by saying that, according to these notions, if a man is not a hypocrite, it does not matter what *religion* he belongs to. By this logic, not only are sincere *Quakers*, *Ranters*, *Muggletonians*, and *Fifth Monarchy-Men* <note>These were radical religious sects in 17th-century England; the author uses them as examples of groups considered extreme or heretical to show the perceived absurdity of the Bishop's logic</note> just as much in the favor of God as any of the *Apostles*, but so are sincere *Jews* and *Turks* <note>original catchword: "Turks"; in this period, "Turk" was a common term for a Muslim</note>.

Does your Lordship imagine that the Tolands, the [Hickeses], the [Burnets] <note>Refers to John Toland, George Hickes, and likely Gilbert Burnet or Thomas Bennett—figures associated with radical or controversial religious views of the era</note> would spend so much time and effort to justify, praise, and expand upon your Lordship’s ideas if they did not think you were committed to their cause?

Muslims <note>original: "Turks"</note> and *Deists* <note>Those who believe in God based on reason rather than revelation</note> are on as good a foundation <note>original: "Bottom"</note> and as secure in the favor of God as the most sincere Christian.

For your Lordship says it is *sincerity*, on its own, that procures the favor of God. If it is *sincerity* on its own, then it is *sincerity* independent and exclusive of any particular way of worship. And if the *favor of God equally follows* every equal *degree of sincerity*, then it is impossible there should be any difference, either in *merit* or *happiness*, between a sincere *martyr* and a sincere *persecutor*. Thus, he that burns the Christian—if he is only in earnest—has the same title to a reward for it as he who is burnt for believing in Christ.

Your Lordship says you cannot help it if people charge you with <note>The asterisk points to the footnote below.</note> *evil intentions* and *bad views*. I intend no such charge. But I wonder that your Lordship should think it hard that anyone should infer from these passages that you are against the *interest of the Church of England*.

You tell all sorts of people that if they are merely sincere in their own way, they are as much in God’s favor as anyone else. Is this supporting our interests <note>original: "Interest"; referring to the welfare and standing of the established Church</note>, my Lord?

Suppose a friend of King George <note>King George I, whose right to the throne was contested during this period</note> should declare to all *Britons* <note>original: "Britains"</note> whatsoever that, although they were divided into five thousand different parties to set up different *Pretenders* <note>Claimants to the throne who challenged the ruling monarch, specifically the Jacobite "Old Pretender"</note>, yet if they were only sincere in their designs, they would be as much in the favor of God as those who are most firmly attached to his *Majesty*. Does your Lordship think such a person would be thought a great friend to the government? And, my Lord, is this not the very declaration you made regarding the Church of *England*?

Have you not told all parties that their sincerity is enough? Have you said even one word to recommend our communion <note>The Church of England</note>? Or, if it were not for your church title <note>original: "Church-Character"</note> on the *title page* of this discourse, could anyone alive conceive what communion you belonged to? Indeed, a reader who was a stranger would imagine that he who will allow no difference between communions is himself of no communion. Your Lordship, for all I know, may act according to the strictest sincerity and may think it your duty to undermine the foundations of the Church. I am only surprised that you should refuse to acknowledge the reasonableness of such a charge.

Your Lordship has <note>original: "hath"</note> canceled all our obligations to any particular communion under the pretext of sincerity.

I hope, my Lord, there is mercy in store for all sorts of people, however erroneous <note>original: "erroneous"; meaning mistaken or straying from the truth</note> in their way of worshiping God; but I cannot believe that to be a sincere Christian is to be no more in the favor of God than to be a sincere *Deist* <term>Deism is the belief in a creator who does not intervene in the universe, often rejecting the divinity of Christ and the authority of the Bible</term>, or a sincere *destroyer* of Christians. It will be allowed that sincerity is a necessary principle of true religion, and that without it, all the most impressive appearances of virtue are worth nothing. But still, neither common sense nor plain Scripture will allow me to think that when our Savior was on Earth, those who sincerely refused to be his disciples and sincerely called for his crucifixion were as much in the favor of God as those who sincerely left everything and followed him. If they were, my Lord, where is that blessedness of believing so often mentioned in the Scripture? Or where is the happiness of the Gospel revelation, if those who sincerely refuse it are as well off as those who embrace it with integrity?

Our Savior declared that those who believed should be saved, but those who did not believe should be damned. Will your Lordship say that all unbelievers were insincere? Or that, though they were damned, they were yet in the same favor with God as those who were saved?

The Apostle assures us *that there is no other name under heaven given to men by which they can be saved, but Jesus Christ* <note>original: "there is no other Name under Heaven given unto Men, whereby they can be saved, but Jesus Christ"; referencing Acts 4:12</note>. My Lord, I am not exaggerating your meaning. If sincerity, as such, is the only thing that recommends us to God, and every equal degree of it earns an equal degree of favor, then it is a demonstration that sincerity *against* Christ is as pleasing to God as sincerity *for* him. <meta>This page continues the author's critique of the Bishop of Bangor’s views on "sincerity." The author argues that sincerity can be the result of one's own faults or divine judgment, and therefore cannot be the sole measure of God's favor.</meta>

It may be due to our own conduct—some irregularities or the abuse of our mental faculties—that we perceive things as we do and are fixed in certain tenets. Can we really believe that so much value is owed to a *sincerity* of opinion when that sincerity was formed through bad *habits* and guilty behavior? There are several faulty ways people can cloud and bias their own understanding, throwing themselves into a very strange way of thinking; for some reason or another, *God may send them a strong delusion so that they believe a lie.* <note>original: "God may send them a strong Delusion that they should believe a Lie"; a reference to 2 Thessalonians 2:11</note>

And will your Lordship <note>Referring to Benjamin Hoadly, the Bishop of Bangor</note> really say that those who have fallen into such errors—perhaps through their own poor conduct or as a judgment of God upon them—are as much in His favor as those who love and stick to the truth? This, my Lord, is a shocking opinion. It has caused great offense to many Christians because it contradicts common sense and plain Scripture by putting all religions on the same level regarding the favor of God.

The next thing we should not be concerned about, according to your Lordship, is *the "vain words" of regular and uninterrupted successions, which you dismiss as "niceties, trifles, and dreams."* <note>This refers to Apostolic Succession: the doctrine that church authority is passed down in an unbroken chain from the original Apostles to modern bishops.</note> Surely, this much is implied in these words: that no kind of *ordination or mission of the clergy* <term>Mission: The formal authority or "sending out" of a minister by the church to preach and administer the sacraments</term> is of any consequence or importance to us. For if ordination does not need to be *regular*—meaning derived from those who received authority from Christ to ordain others—then it is clear that no specific type of ordination can be more valuable than any other. After all, no ordination could have a worse defect than being *irregular* and not derived through a succession from Christ. Therefore, if these circumstances are to be viewed as *trifles and dreams*, then any difference that can be imagined between any ordina-

Therefore, *Quakers*, *Independents*, and *Presbyterians*, according to your Lordship, have as much reason to think their teachers are useful to them—and are true *ministers of Christ*—as those in the *Episcopal communion* <note>The Church of England and other churches governed by bishops.</note> have to believe in their own teachers.

For if the *regularity of ordination* and *uninterrupted succession* <note>Apostolic Succession: The doctrine that church authority is passed down in an unbroken chain from the Apostles to modern bishops.</note> are merely *trifles* and amount to nothing, then every difference between us and other teachers must also be nothing, because they can differ from us in no other way. Thus, my Lord, if the *Church of England* has fought for the necessity of *episcopal ordination* derived from *Christ*, you have deserted her on this point. You not only abandon *episcopal ordination* by ridiculing the idea of a *succession*, but by the same *argument*, you prevent any *ministers* on earth from possessing *Christ’s* authority.

For if there is not a *succession* of people authorized by *Christ* to send others to act in His name, then both *Episcopal* and *Presbyterian* <note>Presbyterians believe in a church governed by elders (presbyters) rather than bishops.</note> teachers are equally *usurpers* <term>Usurper: Someone who wrongfully takes a position of power or authority without a legal or divine right.</term>, and are as much mere *laymen* as anyone else. For there can be no other difference between the *clergy* and the *laity* <note>The "laity" refers to the ordinary members of a church who are not ordained as clergy.</note> except that the former has authority derived from *Christ* to perform offices which the latter does not.

But this authority can be obtained in no other way than through an *uninterrupted succession* of men from *Christ*, empowered to qualify others. For if the *succession* is ever broken, people must either enter the *ministry* of their own accord, or be sent by those who have no more power to send others than they have to go themselves. And, my Lord, can such people be called *ministers of Christ*, or re[ceived...]

To make a joke, therefore, of *uninterrupted succession* is to make a joke of ordination. It destroys the sacred character of the office and makes all pretenders to it just as valid as those who are truly sent by Christ.

If there is no *uninterrupted succession*, then there are no authorized ministers from Christ. If there are no such ministers, then there are no Christian sacraments. ### Absolute

When Dr. Snape <note>Dr. Andrew Snape (1675–1742) was a high-church clergyman and one of Hoadly's chief opponents in the Bangorian Controversy.</note> said that no church authority was to be obeyed in anything contrary to the revealed will of God, your Lordship <note>Referring to Benjamin Hoadly, the Bishop of Bangor.</note> triumphs in this way: *"Glorious absolute <note>original: "Absolute" — here meaning total, unconditional power that requires unquestioning obedience.</note> authority, indeed, by your own account; an authority to which Christ's subjects owe no obedience until they have examined his own declarations; and then they obey not this authority, but him."* *

Here, you make nothing of any authority that is not *absolute*; and yet you think it is unfair to be told that you have taken away all *church authority*. You explicitly deny that which is *absolute*, and here you say that which is *not* absolute is nothing at all. Where, then, is the *authority* you have left? Or how is it that Christ has empowered anyone to act in his name?

Your Lordship fights safely under the protection of the word *absolute*, but your real aim is to destroy all church power. Your Lordship makes too hasty an inference <note>An inference is a logical conclusion drawn from evidence.</note>—namely, that because authority is not *absolute*, it is nothing at all. If you ask where you have made this inference, it is on the occasion of the triumph mentioned above, where your Lordship portrays it as an insignificant authority if it is only to be obeyed so long as it is not contrary to Scripture.

Your Lordship seems to think that all is lost regarding church power because the Doctor <note>Referring to Dr. Andrew Snape, whose defense of church authority Hoadly had attacked.</note> does not claim an *absolute power* but allows it to be subject to *Scripture*. I shall, therefore, consider the nature of this church power and show that although it is not *absolute*, it is still a *real authority* and is not the mere abstraction that your Lordship makes it out to be.

An *absolute authority*, according to your Lordship, is one that must always be obeyed by every individual subject to it, in all circumstances. ## My LORD,

<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap 'A' within a square frame. The background of the frame depicts a landscape scene with an archway or building, a tree, and a radiating sun in the upper right corner.</image-desc> A sincere concern for truth and the fundamental principles of the Christian religion was the only motive that led me to examine your Lordship’s doctrines in a previous letter to you. I hope that same motive will be seen as a sufficient apology for my taking the liberty of giving your Lordship the trouble of a second letter.

<margin>* *A Preservative*, page 98.</margin> <margin>† Page 89.</margin> <margin>|| Page 101.</margin>
Among the useless and contemptible things for which your Lordship would have the laity <note>laity: ordinary people who are not members of the clergy</note> feel an abhorrence are "the *trifles and fine details of authoritative blessings, absolutions, and excommunications*." <note>original: "Authoritative Benedictions, Absolutions, Excommunications"—the formal spiritual actions of a priest, such as pronouncing forgiveness or removing someone from the church community</note> Again, you say "that to expect the grace of God from any hands but His own is to insult Him." And you state "that everything depends upon God and ourselves; that human blessings, human absolutions, and human excommunications have nothing to do with the favor of God."

It is evident from these principles (for your Lordship states them as such) that whatever rituals are observed in any Christian society based on the assumption that grace is given through *human hands*, or by the ministry of the clergy, such rituals should be condemned—and are indeed condemned by your Lordship—as trifling, useless, and insulting to God.

There is a rite, my Lord, in the still-established Church of England which we call *Confirmation*. It is founded upon the clear words of Scripture, the practice of the early Church <note>original: "Primitive Observance"—the customs and rituals followed by the very first generations of Christians</note>, and the universal practice of every following age in the Church. The purpose of this rite is that it should serve as a means of

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of the Bishop's views on clergy. The previous page ended mid-sentence, discussing rituals "based on the assumption..." this page completes that thought.</meta>

of conferring grace through prayer and the laying on of the *Bishop’s hands* on those who have already been baptized. Yet, against all this authority—both divine and human—and the explicit order of our own Church, your Lordship teaches the laity <note>laity: ordinary people who are not members of the clergy</note> *that all human blessings are useless fine details, and that to expect God’s grace from any hands but His own is to insult Him.*

If so, my Lord, how shall we defend the Apostles? We read in Acts 8:14 that when *Philip* the Deacon had baptized the *Samaritans*, the Apostles sent *Peter* and *John* to them. These two, after they had prayed and *laid their hands on them, received the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note>, who previously had not fallen upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.*

My Lord, several things here are beyond question:

*First*, that something else—even in the time of the Apostles—was necessary besides baptism to qualify people to become complete members of the body of Christ, or partakers of His grace. They had been baptized, yet they did not receive the Holy Spirit until the Apostles’ hands were laid upon them.

*Second*, that God’s graces are conferred not only through *human hands*, but through some specific hands and not others.

*Third*, that this office <note>office: a formal religious ceremony or duty</note> was so strictly reserved for the Apostles, or the chief governors of the Church, that it could not be performed by inspired men of a lower rank, even though they were empowered to work miracles, such as *Philip* the Deacon.

*Fourth*, that the power of the Apostles to perform this ordinance <note>ordinance: a religious rite or ritual</note> was entirely due to their higher rank in the ministry, and not to any extraordinary spiritual gifts they possessed. For if gifts were the cause, *Philip* could have performed it; he did not lack those gifts, being himself an evangelist <note>evangelist: in the early church, a traveling minister or preacher</note> and a worker of miracles. This is a demonstration that his inability to perform the rite arose from his lower rank in the ministry.

And now, my Lord, are all *human blessings merely fine details and trifles*? Are the means of God’s grace in His own hands alone? Is it wicked and offensive to God to suppose the contrary? How then did *Peter* and *John* bestow the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> by the laying on of their hands <note>original: "Imposition of their Hands"</note>? Why did they claim this specific office <note>office: a formal religious duty or role</note> for themselves? Is the distribution of God’s grace in *His own hands alone*? And yet, can it be dispensed to us through the ministry of some people, and not by others?

Were the Apostles so wicked that they tried to distinguish themselves by claiming empty powers which God had reserved for Himself? According to the title of your book, the *Preservative* <note>The Bishop of Bangor’s 1716 work, *A Preservative Against the Principles and Practices of the Non-jurors*</note>, your Lordship supposes that it is inconsistent with *common sense* to imagine that God would or could have communicated such powers to men.

If any of your Lordship’s well-instructed laity <note>laity: church members who are not ordained clergy</note> had lived in the days of the Apostles, they would have surely rejected this senseless, imaginary <note>original: "chimerical"</note> *claim of the Apostles* with great indignation. They would have said, "Why do you, *Peter* or *John*, pretend to have this blasphemous power? *As long as we believe the Gospel, we cannot expect the grace of God from any hands but His own.* You give us the *Holy Spirit*! You bestow the grace of God! Is it not impious to think that He should make our *improvement in grace* depend upon your ministry, or hang our salvation on any particular order of clergymen? We know that God is just, and good, and true, and that everything depends upon Him and ourselves, and that *human blessings* are *trifles*. Therefore, whether you, *Peter*, or you, *Philip*, or both, or neither of you lay your hands upon us, we are neither better nor worse; we remain in the *same state of grace* as we were before."

This representation does not contain a single syllable that is not founded upon your Lordship’s own doctrine and perfectly agreeable to it.

<meta>This page continues William Law’s critique of the Bishop of Bangor’s views on church authority. Law argues that if the Bishop believes human blessings are "trifles," then his own practice of confirmation is either hypocritical or a mockery of the rite.</meta>

The late most pious and learned Bishop *Beveridge* <note>William Beveridge (1637–1708) was a prominent Anglican bishop and theologian known for his devotion to the early Church's traditions.</note> has these remarkable words upon *Confirmation*:

> “I do not know how any bishops in our age dare neglect such a significant part of their office; but I fear they will have no good account to give of it when they come to stand before God’s tribunal.” <note>original: *First Volume of Sermons.*</note>

But we may justly, and therefore I hope with decency, ask your Lordship: how do you dare perform this part of your office? For you have condemned it as *trivial* <note>original: "Trifling"</note> and *wicked*; as trivial because it is a *human blessing* <note>original: "human Benediction"</note>, and as wicked because it assumes grace is conferred by the *hands of the bishop*. If, therefore, any baptized persons should come to your Lordship for confirmation, and if you are *sincere* in what you have delivered, your Lordship ought, I humbly suggest, to make this declaration to them:

> “My friends, for the sake of *decency* and *order*, I have taken upon myself the role of a bishop <note>original: "Epiſcopal Character"</note>; and, according to custom—which has long prevailed against common sense—I am now to lay my hands upon you. But I beg you, as you have any regard for the truth of the Gospel or for the honor of God, do not imagine there is anything in this action more than a useless, empty ceremony. For if you expect to have any spiritual advantage from *human blessings*, or to receive grace from the *laying on* <note>original: "Imposition"</note> of a bishop’s hands, you insult God and, in effect, renounce Christianity.”

--- Page 57 ---
<meta>This page continues William Law’s argument against the Bishop of Bangor’s dismissal of church rituals. Law is using the ritual of Confirmation to demonstrate that the Bible treats "human blessings"—which the Bishop calls useless—as fundamental principles of the Christian faith.</meta>

<page-num>[ 7 ]</page-num>
<sig>A 4</sig>

My Lord, here it is undeniably clear that this laying on of hands (which we call *Confirmation*) is such a fundamental part of Christ’s religion that it is called one of the first principles of the doctrine of Christ. It is ranked alongside such primary truths as the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment.

St. *Cyprian* <note>St. Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD) was the Bishop of Carthage and an influential early Christian writer who emphasized the unity of the Church.</note>, speaking of this apostolic laying on of hands, says:
> *The same practice is now observed among us; those who have been baptized in the Church are brought to the leaders <note>original: "Presidents"</note> of the Church, so that by our prayer and the laying on of hands, they may receive the Holy Spirit and be perfected <note>original: "consummated"</note> with the Lord’s seal.*

Must we still believe, then, that all *human blessings* <note>original: "human Benedictions"</note> are merely dreams, and that the laying on of human hands is trivial and useless? Must we believe that to expect God’s grace through them is an insult to Him? This is despite the fact that the Scriptures explicitly teach us that God confers His grace through specific *human hands*, and not through others. They tell us that this *human blessing*—this laying on of hands—is one of the first principles of the religion of Christ, and as much a foundational doctrine as the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment. In this rite, through a human blessing and the laying on of the bishop’s hands, the Holy Spirit is believed to be conferred upon individuals to consecrate them for the work of the ministry.

<meta>This page continues William Law’s critique of the Bishop of Bangor. Law is now using the Church of England’s own official liturgy to point out the logical inconsistency in the Bishop’s argument that human mediation in divine grace is an "affront" to God.</meta>

In keeping with the meaning of Scripture and the practices of the early Church <note>original: "Antiquity"</note>, our Church uses this form of ordination: *The Bishop, laying his hands on the person's head, says, "Receive the Holy Spirit for the office and work of a priest in the Church of God, now committed to you by the laying on of our hands."* From this form, three things are clear: *First*, that our Church holds that receiving the Holy Spirit is necessary to make a person a Christian priest. *Second*, that the Holy Spirit is bestowed through *human* hands. *Third*, that it is specifically by the hands of a bishop that the Holy Spirit is bestowed.

Therefore, if your Lordship is correct in your doctrine, the *Church of England* is clearly very corrupt. For if it is dishonorable and insulting to God to expect His grace from any human hands, it must necessarily be dishonorable and insulting to Him for a bishop to claim to bestow it by his hands. And can that Church be defended in any way, having established such a sin <note>original: "Iniquity"</note> by law and made this ritual so essential? 

How can your Lordship justify to your laypeople <note>the non-clergy members of the church</note> accepting the status and power of a bishop through such a form of words? You tell them it is insulting to God to expect His grace from *human hands*; yet, to qualify yourself for a bishopric <note>the office or rank of a bishop</note>, you allowed human hands to be laid on you in a manner that directly assumes you received the *Holy Spirit* through them! Is it wicked for them to expect grace from *human hands*? And is it any less so for your Lordship to claim to receive it from human hands? 

Anyone who believes it is insulting to God to expect His grace from human hands must also believe that our form of ordination—which promises the Holy Spirit through the *bishop's hands*—must also be insulting to God. Certainly, a man cannot be said to be very protective of God’s honor if he submits himself to be made a bishop by a ritual which, according to his own principles, is derogatory to that honor.

<meta>This page continues William Law’s defense of the established clergy against Bishop Hoadly. Law argues that the clergy do not claim arbitrary power over salvation but act as God's authorized representatives, similar to the biblical roles of Abraham and Job.</meta>

...[whom God] pleases to save; nor do they claim that they have the arbitrary control <note>original: "Disposal"</note> over the happiness of mankind. Neither, my Lord, do the **Christian Clergy** claim this kind of despotic <note>original: "despotick"</note> empire over their flocks. They do not claim for themselves a power to damn the innocent or to save the guilty; rather, they assert a serious and just right to reconcile people to God and to act in His name in restoring them to His favor. They received their commission <term>commission: a formal granting of authority to perform certain religious duties</term> from those whom **Christ** sent with full authority to send others, along with a promise that He would be with them until the end of the world. From this, they conclude that they have His authority. Consequently, they believe their ministry <note>original: "Administrations"</note> is necessary and effective for the salvation of mankind. They believe that no one can despise them without also despising Him who sent them. Furthermore, they believe people are as certainly outside the Covenant of Grace <term>Covenant of Grace: the biblical promise that God will show favor and salvation to those who have faith</term> when they abandon His pastors as when they openly despise or fail to receive His sacraments.

And what is there in this doctrine, my Lord, to terrify the consciences of the **laity**? What is there here to cause the profane scandal of **"priestcraft"** <term>priestcraft: a derogatory term for the perceived use of religious position to gain power or deceive the public</term> to be blamed on the **clergy**? Could there be any reason for Abimelech to hate Abraham because Abraham was the one who was to reconcile him to God? Could Eliphaz justly hold any prejudice against Job because God chose to hear Job’s intercession on his behalf? Why then, my Lord, must the **Christian Prieſthood** be considered such a horrible and hateful institution, when its entire purpose is to restore people to the grace and favor of God? Why must we be abused and insulted for being sent on the errand of salvation and made ministers of eternal happiness to our brothers? There is a woe due to us...

<summary>William Law argues that the clergy’s authority is not a form of personal power but a divine appointment intended for the spiritual benefit and salvation of the laity. He uses biblical examples to show that God often uses specific individuals as mediators for His grace.</summary>

<meta>This page continues William Law’s defense of the ministerial authority of the clergy. He argues that the human failings of priests do not invalidate their God-given role, just as the weaknesses of biblical figures like Abraham or the Apostles did not undermine their divine commissions.</meta>

[ 19 ]

<sig>B 2</sig>

...[woe to] us if we do not preach the Gospel, or if we neglect those ministerial duties <note>original: "Offices"</note> that Christ has entrusted to us. We are to watch over their souls as those who must give an account to God. Why then must we be treated as arrogant priests, or as "popishly" <note>original: "popishly affected"; meaning having sympathies for the Roman Catholic Church</note> inclined, simply for claiming <note>original: "pretending"</note> to have a role in the salvation of men through the exercise of our ***ministry***? Why must we be rebuked <note>original: "reproached"</note> for ***blasphemous claims*** and ***absurd, senseless powers*** because we take it upon ourselves to bless in God’s name, or because we think our religious services <note>original: "Administrations"</note> are more effective than the actions of an ordinary ***layperson***?

Furthermore, why does your Lordship object to these powers in the ***clergy*** based on the fact that they share the same human weaknesses and failings as the rest of mankind? Were not ***Abraham***, ***Job***, and the ***Jewish*** priests men with the same passions as us? Did our ***Saviour*** not command the ***Jews*** to look to their priests, despite their personal faults, because they sat in ***Moses’s chair*** <term>Moses's chair: a symbol of religious and legal authority in the Jewish tradition</term>? Did the ***apostles*** not assure their followers that they were men of like passions as they were? But did they, because of this, renounce their mission or their apostolic authority? Did they teach that their natural weaknesses made them any less the ministers of God, or any less necessary for the salvation of men?

Their personal defects did not make them abandon the claim to those powers they were granted, nor did they desert their ministry. Instead, these flaws gave ***St. Paul*** the opportunity to say, *“We have this treasure in earthen vessels (meaning this authority is committed to mere men), so that the excellence of it may be from God and not from men.”* The Apostle’s view differs very much from your Lordship’s: he says such weak instruments were used so that the glory would go to God. Your Lordship says that to suppose such instruments provide any benefit to us is to diminish the sovereignty of God and, consequently, His glory.

Your Lordship imagines you have sufficiently destroyed the *priestly powers* <note>original: "sacerdotal Powers"</note> by showing that the clergy are only men and subject to the common frailties of mankind. My Lord, we admit to this charge, and we do not claim any *priestly powers* based on our personal abilities or to gain any glory for ourselves. But, weak as we are, we are God's ministers; and if we are either afraid or ashamed of our duty, we must perish in that guilt. But is a prophet therefore proud because he insists upon the authority of his mission? Can a mortal not be God's *messenger* and employed in His affairs without being called insolent and arrogant for having the courage to admit it? If we are to be rebuked <note>original: "reprov'd"</note> for claiming <note>original: "pretending"</note> to be God's ministers simply because we are only men, the blame will fall upon Providence; since it has pleased God to conduct His affairs with mankind primarily through the ministry of their fellow human beings.

Your Lordship does not have a single word from Scripture against these *priestly powers*; you have no proof that Christ has not sent men to be effective administrators of His grace. You only assert that there can be no such *ministers* because they are merely men.

Now, my Lord, I must take the liberty to say that if the natural weakness of men makes them incapable of being the instruments for conveying grace to their brethren; if the clergy cannot be of any use or necessity to their flocks for this reason; then it follows undeniably that there can be no *positive institutions* <term>positive institutions: religious duties or rites established by divine command rather than natural law, such as the sacraments</term> in the *Christian religion* that can provide any spiritual advantages to its members. In that case, the sacraments can no longer be any *means of grace* <term>means of grace: outward signs or rituals through which God conveys spiritual blessing</term>. For I hope no one thinks that bread and wine have any natural force or effectiveness to convey grace to the soul. The water in *Baptism* has the common qualities of water and lacks any inherent <note>original: "intrinsick"</note> power to cleanse the soul or purify it from sin. But your Lordship will not say that because...

If water has only the common nature of water, then—by your logic—it cannot be a means of grace <term>means of grace: a ritual or practice through which God’s spiritual help or favor is believed to be given</term>. And now, my Lord, let the common sense of mankind judge: if the clergy are thought to have no authority because they are only men, does it not plainly follow that everything else must be rejected too? Must we not also reject every institution that does not have some *natural* force and power to produce the effects intended for it as being equally trivial and ineffective?

To summarize the matter: It is clear from many specific facts—and indeed, from the entire course of God's Providence <term>God's Providence: the protective care and spiritual guidance provided by God</term>—that it is not only consistent with His nature but also fits His usual way of dealing with mankind that He should appoint men to act in His name. These men are *authoritatively* employed to give His grace and favors to humanity.

It appears that your Lordship's argument against the authoritative work <note>original: "Administrations"</note> of the Christian clergy does more than just contradict these facts and condemn the usual method of God's dealings <term>God's dispensations: the divine system or body of laws by which God governs the world or a specific era</term> with us. It also proves the sacraments and every established practice of Christianity to be ineffective. It treats them as mere *dreams* and *trivialities*, just like the various *roles* and *ranks* of the clergy.

This, I hope, will be considered a sufficient refutation of your Lordship's doctrine by all who have any true regard or zeal for the Christian religion and who only expect to be saved by the methods of divine grace proposed in the Gospel.

<meta>This page continues Law’s argument that spiritual authority is divinely appointed. He transitions from discussing the sacraments to the specific "Sacredness of the Ecclesiastical Character" (the priestly office), arguing that it is established by the Holy Spirit rather than human convention.</meta>

[ 23 ]

I will now briefly set forth the sacredness of the ecclesiastical <note>original: "Ecclesiastical Character" — refers to the spiritual status or "indelible mark" of a priest</note> role, as it is founded in the New Testament; I will pay particular attention to the power of bestowing grace and the effectiveness of human blessings <note>original: "Benedictions"</note>.

It appears in the New Testament that all priestly <note>original: "sacerdotal"</note> power is derived from the Holy Spirit. Our Savior himself did not take that ministry upon himself until he had received this consecration. And during the time of his ministry, he was under the guidance and direction of the Holy Spirit. Through the Holy Spirit, he gave commands to the apostles whom he had chosen. When he ordained them to the work of the ministry, he did so with these words, *Receive the Holy Spirit*. Those whom the apostles ordained to the same role were appointed by the same authority: they laid their hands upon the elders, urging them to take care of the flock of Christ, over which the Holy Spirit had made them overseers.

By this, they plainly declared that although this office was to descend from person to person through *human hands*, it was the Holy Spirit who consecrated them for that employment and gave them authority to perform it.

From this, it is also obvious that the priesthood is a gift <note>original: "Grace" — in this context, a spiritual gift or office granted by God</note> of the Holy Spirit. It is not a function based on the natural or civil rights of mankind, but is derived from the special authority of the Holy Spirit; it is as truly a positive institution <term>positive institution: a practice or law established by a specific divine command rather than by natural reason alone</term> as the sacraments. So, those who have no authority to change the old sacraments and substitute new ones have no power to change the ancient order of the clergy or introduce any other order of them.

For why can we not change the sacraments? Is it not because they are only sacraments—and only function—insofar as they are established by the Holy Spirit? Because they are useless, ineffective rituals without this divine authority?

<meta>This page continues William Law’s critique of Bishop Benjamin Hoadly’s "Preservative Against the Principles and Practices of the Nonjurors." Law is now shifting his focus from church structure to the specific doctrine of absolution, challenging Hoadly’s argument that fallible humans cannot exercise divine authority.</meta>

The next thing to consider, my Lord, is your doctrine concerning absolutions <term>absolution: the formal release from guilt or forgiveness of sins, pronounced by a priest</term>. You begin as follows:

> *You will find that the same argument provides a sufficient reply to their arrogant claim to an authoritative absolution. An infallible absolution cannot belong to fallible men. But no absolution can be authoritative if it is not infallible. Therefore, no authoritative absolution can belong to any living person.*\*

I must observe here, your Lordship, that you do not reject this *absolution* because the claim for it is not found in Scripture; instead, you use an argument based on the nature of the thing itself. Because you imagine that such an absolution requires infallibility <term>infallibility: the quality of being incapable of making mistakes or being wrong</term> to carry it out, you conclude it cannot belong to human beings. If this were true, it would prove that even if our Savior had truly intended to do so, He could not have given this power to His ministers. 

But, my Lord, who can see any contradiction <note>original: "Repugnancy"</note> in the logic of the thing itself? Is it not just as easy to imagine that our Lord would grant His grace of pardon through the hands of His ministers as He does through the sacraments <note>original: "Sacraments" — Christian rites such as Baptism or Communion believed to be a means of divine grace</note>? And may not such an absolution be rightly called *authoritative* when its power is granted and carried out by His authority?

Is it impossible for humans to have this authority from God simply because they might make mistakes when using it? This argument proves too much; it would destroy every Christian institution just as easily as it destroys this power of absolution.

For if it is impossible for men to have authority from God to forgive sins in His name because they are not infallible, then they are equally incapable of being entrusted with any other means of grace. Consequently, this suggests that the entire concept of the priest’s office <note>original: "Priest's Office" — the duties and authority given to a member of the clergy</note> is a direct impossibility in its very definition.

<meta>This page continues William Law’s critique of Bishop Hoadly. Law argues that if Hoadly's logic regarding the impossibility of fallible men granting absolution were true, it would also invalidate the sacraments and the entire structure of the Christian religion.</meta>

<sig>C</sig>

Your Lordship’s argument is this: Christians have their sins pardoned upon certain conditions, but fallible <term>fallible: capable of making mistakes or being wrong</term> men cannot certainly know if these conditions have been met. Therefore, fallible men cannot have the authority to *absolve* <note>original: "absolve" — to formally pronounce forgiveness of sins</note>.

From this, I take the opportunity to argue as follows: Persons are to be admitted to the sacraments <note>original: "Sacraments" — religious rites like Baptism and Holy Communion</note> based on certain conditions; but fallible men cannot tell whether those people come qualified to receive them according to these conditions. Therefore, fallible men cannot have the authority to administer the sacraments.

Secondly, this argument undermines all authority of the Christian religion itself, and the purpose of every instituted means of grace <term>means of grace: sacred acts or rituals through which it is believed God’s blessing and assistance are transmitted to people</term>. For if nothing can be authoritative unless a person is infallibly assured of it, then the Christian religion cannot be an authoritative method of salvation; since a person, by being a Christian, does not become infallibly certain of his salvation. Nor does grace infallibly accompany the participation in the sacraments. 

So, although your Lordship has formed this argument only against this power of absolution, it has just as much force against the sacraments and the Christian religion itself. For if it is absurd to assume that a priest should absolve anyone because he cannot be certain that the person deserves absolution, does it not imply the same absurdity to assume that he should have the power of administering the sacraments, when he cannot be *infallibly certain* that those who receive them are properly qualified? If a possibility of error destroys the power in one case, it just as certainly destroys it in the other. Again, if absolution cannot be authoritative unless it is infallible, then it is plain that the Christian religion is not an authoritative means of salvation, because all Christians are not infallibly saved; nor can the sacraments be authoritative means of grace, because everyone who partakes in them does not infallibly obtain grace.

Your Lordship proceeds to address your laypeople <note>original: "Laity" — members of the church who are not ordained clergy</note> by way of protest: *If they distract <note>original: "amuse" — in the 18th century, this often meant to divert attention, delude, or bewilder rather than to entertain</note> you with that power which Christ left with his Apostles: "Whosoever’s sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whosoever’s sins you retain, they are retained."*\*

This statement must be true, or else there is no weight or *confidence* in the objection you raise here for the instruction of the laypeople. If it is well-founded, then the clergy cannot possibly prove they have any more right to exercise any part of their office than the laypeople do. Do they claim to ordain, confirm, or to admit or exclude men from the sacraments? By what authority is all this done? Is it not because the Apostles, whose successors they are, did the same things? <meta>This page begins a postscript to William Law’s first letter to the Bishop of Bangor. Law transitions from his main argument to addressing specific objections regarding the "uninterrupted succession" of the clergy—the idea that authority is passed down in an unbroken chain from the Apostles.</meta>

[ 66 ]

## P O S T S C R I P T.

I hope your Lordship will not think it unnatural or irrelevant to offer here a word or two in answer to some objections against my previous letter.

To begin with the doctrine of the uninterrupted succession of the clergy <note>The belief that validly ordained bishops can trace their spiritual authority in a direct, unbroken line back to the original Apostles</note>.

I believe I have proved that a divine commission is required to qualify anyone to exercise the priestly office. Since this divine commission can only be obtained from those specific persons whom God has appointed to give it, it is therefore necessary that there should be a continual succession of such persons in order to maintain a commissioned order of clergy. For if the commission itself is to descend through the ages and distinguish the clergy from the laity <note>The ordinary members of the church, as distinguished from the clergy</note>, it is certain that the persons who alone can give this commission must descend through the same ages. Consequently, an uninterrupted succession is as necessary as it is for the clergy to have a divine commission. 

If you take away this succession, the clergy might as well be ordained by one person as another; a group of women might just as well give them a divine commission as a congregation of any men. ## POSTSCRIPT.

I hope your Lordship will not think it unnatural or inappropriate <note>original: "impertinent"</note> to offer a word or two here in answer to some objections against my former letter.

To begin with the doctrine of the uninterrupted succession of the clergy:

I believe I have proved that a divine commission is required to qualify anyone to exercise the priestly office. Since this divine commission can only be obtained from those specific people whom God has appointed to grant it, it is therefore necessary for there to be a continual succession of such people in order to maintain a commissioned order of the clergy. For if the commission itself is to descend through the ages and distinguish the clergy from the laity, it is certain that the people who alone can grant this commission must descend through those same ages. Consequently, an uninterrupted succession is as necessary as the clergy having a divine commission in the first place. 

If you take away this succession, then the clergy might as well be ordained by one person as another. A group of women might as well give them a divine commission as a congregation of any men. They might indeed appoint people to officiate in holy orders for the sake of *decency* and *order*, but that would be nothing more than an external *decency* and *order*. They would be no more the priests of God than those who pretended to make them so. If we had lost the Scriptures, it would be all well and good to write the best books we could and come as close to them as possible, but it would be not only folly but presumption to call them the Word of God. 

But I proceed to the objections against the doctrine of an uninterrupted succession.

*First*, it is said that there is no mention made of it in Scripture as having any relation to the existence <note>original: "Being"</note> of a church.

<meta>This page continues the argument that while not all apostolic practices are permanent, some (like episcopacy) are essential. It challenges the "all or nothing" logical fallacy used by opponents of church hierarchy.</meta>

<page-num>74</page-num>

[...from one ex]treme into another, as if there were no such thing as a middle way, or any such virtue as *moderation*. Thus, either the church must have an *absolute, uncontrollable authority*, or none at all; we must either hold *all* apostolic practices to be necessary, or *none at all*.

Again, if no apostolic *practices* can be unalterable simply because all of them are not, then no apostolic *doctrines* are necessary to be taught in all ages, because all apostolic *doctrines* are not. By this logic, we are no more obliged to teach the *death, satisfaction* <note>original: "Satisfaction"; the theological concept that Christ's death paid the debt for human sin</note>, and *resurrection* of *Jesus Christ* than we are obliged to forbid the *eating of blood and things strangled* <note>referring to a temporary decree in Acts 15:29 intended to help Jewish and Gentile Christians eat together; the author argues that just because this rule was temporary doesn't mean all apostolic teachings are</note>. For if there is anything in the nature of *doctrines*, in the *tenor* <term>the general character, meaning, or direction</term> of *Scripture*, or the *sense* of *antiquity* <note>the teachings and traditions of the early church fathers</note> by which we can know the difference between some *doctrines* and others—that some were *occasional, temporary determinations* suited to particular states and conditions in the church, while others were such general *doctrines* as would concern the church in all states and circumstances—if there can be this difference between apostolic *doctrines*, there must necessarily be the same difference between apostolic *practices*, unless we wish to say that their *practices* were not suited to their *doctrines*. For temporary *doctrines* must produce temporary *practices*.

Now, can we not be obliged by some *practices* of the apostles—where the nature of the matter and the consensus of antiquity show them to be equally necessary and important in all ages and conditions of the church—without being tied down to the strict observance of everything the apostles did, even when it plainly appears that it was done for accidental and changeable reasons? <meta>This page continues the author's argument that some apostolic traditions are temporary while others are permanent. He specifically focuses on the "divine right" of episcopacy (government by bishops), arguing it is essential to the nature of the Christian priesthood rather than just being a historical habit.</meta>

<page-num>[ 75 ]</page-num>

...without being equally obliged to *lock the doors* where we meet, just because in the Apostles' time they locked them for fear of their enemies.

My Lord, we should follow the *practices* of the Apostles, as we ought to follow everything else, with *discretion* and *judgment*. We should not rush headlong into everything they did simply because they were Apostles; yet we should not think that because we do not need to follow them in everything, we need not do it in anything. We best imitate them when we act upon the same reasons they acted upon, neither making their occasional *practices* into perpetual *laws*, nor breaking through such general rules as will always have the *same reason* to be observed.

If it is asked how we can know which *practices* must be observed and which may be set aside, I answer: in the same way we distinguish *articles of faith* from *lesser truths*, or how we distinguish *occasional doctrines* from *permanent doctrines*. That is, we know by the *nature* of the things, from the *general character* <term>original: "Tenor"</term> of Scripture, and the *testimony of the early church* <note>original: "Antiquity"</note>.

Secondly, it is not true that the *divine unalterable right of episcopacy* <term>government of the church by bishops</term> is founded *merely* upon apostolic practice.

We do not say that episcopacy cannot be changed *merely* because we have apostolic practice for it, but because of the nature of the Christian priesthood: it can only be continued in that method which God has appointed for its continuation. Thus, episcopacy is the *only* established method of continuing the priesthood; therefore, episcopacy is *unchangeable*. This is not just because it is an apostolic practice, but because the nature of the thing requires it. A formal decree <note>original: "positive Institution"; a law or rite established by specific divine command rather than by natural reason</note> can only be continued in the method that God has appointed. So, it is the nature of the priesthood, and not the apostolic practice alone, that makes it necessary to be continued. Apostolic practice indeed shows that...

<meta>This page continues the author's argument from the previous page: that episcopacy (government by bishops) is not merely an optional habit of the early church, but is fundamental to the very existence of the priesthood because it was the method of succession established by God.</meta>

<page-num>[ 76 ]</page-num>

Episcopacy is the order that is appointed, but it is the nature of the priesthood that assures us that it is *unalterable*. This is because an office that has no significance except by *divine appointment* <term>the belief that an office is authorized directly by God</term> and institution by God can be continued in no other way than the one God has appointed.

The argument proceeds like this: the Christian priesthood is a divine, positive institution. Just as it could only begin by *divine appointment*, it can only descend to *future generations* <note>original: "After-ages"</note> in such a *method* as God has been pleased to appoint.

The Apostles (and your *Lordship admits* <note>original: "owns"</note> that Christ was in *everything they did*) instituted *episcopacy alone*. Therefore, this method of episcopacy is unalterable—not simply because an *apostolic practice* cannot be set aside, but because the priesthood can only descend to *future generations* in a method that is of *divine appointment*.

So the question is not fairly stated when it is asked whether episcopacy, being an apostolic practice, may be set aside. Instead, it should be asked: is it necessary to continue a specific, established method for continuing the priesthood? Is it necessary to observe an appointed order for receiving a commission from God in order to actually receive a commission from Him? If the case were stated this way, as it ought to be for fairness, anyone would soon perceive that we can no more set aside episcopacy and still continue the Christian priesthood than we can alter the *terms of salvation* and still be in a covenant with God.

I come now, my Lord, to the second objection: *that this uninterrupted succession is subject to such great uncertainty that, if it is necessary, we can never say for certain that we are in the church.*

Is there not the same bare possibility in the thing itself—that the Scriptures may be corrupted in some important points—as there is that this succession might be broken? 

But is there any just reason why we should believe or fear that the Scriptures are corrupted simply because there is a physical possibility of it, even though there is all the proof that can be required to the contrary? Why, then, must we set aside the necessity of this succession based on a *bare possibility* of error, even though there is all the proof that can be required that it was never broken, but was strictly maintained?

And until then, I shall content myself with offering this reason to your Lordship for why it is *morally impossible* <note>original: "morally impossible"; in this context, the author means it is so highly improbable based on human behavior and social rules that it is practically impossible.</note> it ever should have broken in all those years from the Apostles to the present time.

The reason is this: it has been an accepted doctrine in every age of the Church that no ordination was valid except for those performed by bishops. This doctrine, my Lord, has been a constant guard upon the *episcopal succession* <term>the continuous line of bishops stretching back to the Apostles</term>. Since it was universally believed that bishops alone could ordain, it was *morally impossible* that any persons could be received as bishops who had not been ordained in that way.

Now, is it not *morally impossible* that in our Church anyone should be made a bishop without *episcopal ordination*? Is there any possibility of forging orders or stealing a bishopric <term>the office or jurisdiction of a bishop</term> by any other trick? No, it is *morally impossible*, because it is an acknowledged doctrine among us that a bishop can only be ordained by other bishops. Now, just as this doctrine must necessarily prevent anyone from becoming a bishop without *episcopal ordination* in our age, it must have had the same effect in every other age as well as ours. Consequently, it is as reasonable to believe that the succession of bishops was not broken in any age since the Apostles as it is to believe that it was not broken in our own kingdom within these last forty years. For the same doctrine which preserves it for forty years may just as well preserve it for four thousand years, if it was equally believed in all that span of time. I presume your Lordship will not deny that this has been the constant doctrine of the Church. I have not entered into a historical defense of it here; this and indeed every other institution of the Christian Church has lately been very well defended from ecclesiastical records by a very excellent and wise writer.*

## On the Nature of the Church.

To begin with your Lordship’s description of a Church: *“The number of men, whether small or great, whether dispersed or united, who truly and sincerely are subjects to Christ alone in matters of salvation.”* <note>original: Sermon, p. 17. This refers to Hoadly's famous 1717 sermon, "The Nature of the Kingdom, or Church, of Christ," which sparked the Bangorian Controversy.</note>

The Learned Committee <note>The Committee of the Convocation of Canterbury, which was tasked with examining Hoadly's sermon for potential heresy.</note> calls this your Lordship’s description of a Church.

Your Lordship answers: *“I am surprised to hear this called my description of* **A** *Church; whereas I intend, in those words, to describe nothing else but the Universal Invisible Church. It is a description, not of* **A** *church, in our modern way of speaking, but of* **THE** *Church, the invisible Church of Christ.”* <note>original: Answer to Representation, p. 70. Hoadly's formal defense against the Committee's report.</note>

<summary>William Law begins his critique of Bishop Hoadly's definition of "the Church," noting Hoadly's defense that his definition applied only to the "Universal Invisible Church" rather than any specific earthly institution.</summary>
<keywords>ecclesiology, Invisible Church, Benjamin Hoadly, Bangorian Controversy, salvation, Committee of the Convocation</keywords>

May we not also wonder, my Lord, that you should so describe *The Church* that it cannot be called *A Church*? If I should say it is a description of no church at all, I have your Lordship’s own admission that it is not *A Church*; so it is something between *a Church* and no church—that is, it is *The Church*.

Suppose, my Lord, someone should have a mind to be part of your Church; if he joins *A Church*, he is wrong; you do not mean *A Church*, but *The Church*. Your Lordship admits that this is not a description of a church according to the modern way of speaking; I humbly presume to call upon your Lordship to show that it is a description according to the ancient way of speaking. To call the total number of believers the *Invisible Church* is a way of speaking no more to be found in the Scriptures than a company of *Pre-Adamites* <note>original: "Præ-Adamites." This refers to the controversial 17th-century theory that humans existed before the biblical Adam. Law is suggesting the term "Invisible Church" is just as unscriptural and speculative.</note>.

There is no doubt that there is an *Invisible Church*—that is, a number of beings who are in covenant with God who are not to be seen by human eyes—and we may be said to be members of this *Invisible Church* as we are entitled to the same hopes and expectations. But to call the number of men and women who believe in Christ and observe his institutions, whether dispersed or united in this visible world—to call these people *The Invisible Church* is as false and groundless as to call

And it is as appropriate to call a group of men practicing ***Law*** or ***Medicine*** <note>original: "Physick."</note> an "Invisible Society of ***Lawyers*** and ***Physicians***" as it is to call the Church on earth the ***Invisible Church***. For all those acts and duties which prove people to be Christians, or the Church of Christ, are as visible and well-known <note>original: "notorious." Are they not visibly under the dominion of the powers of darkness? Are they not visibly outside of Christ’s Church? Must it not, therefore, be as visible who is in this Church as who is not in it?

If anyone should tell us that we are to believe in ***Invisible Scriptures*** and observe ***Invisible Sacraments***, he would have just as much reason and Scripture on his side as your Lordship has for this doctrine. And it would be of the same service to the world to talk of these ***invisibilities*** if the authority of Scripture was in dispute, as it is to describe this ***invisible*** Church when the question is: with which ***visible*** Church we ought to unite?

But since Christ, who certainly understood the nature of his own kingdom, has declared that it is like a net that gathers *every kind of fish*, it is as absurd to say that it consists only of *one* kind of person (namely, the invisibly good) as to say that the net which gathers *every kind* has only *one* kind in it. Now, just as it was both the bad and the good fish which filled the net, and the Church is compared to the net in this respect, it is evident that bad men as well as good are subjects of this kingdom. And I assume they are members of that kingdom which they fill up, just as surely as the fish must be in the net before they can fill it. All these circumstances plainly declare that the Church, or Kingdom of Christ, shall consist of a mixture of good and bad people until the end of the world.

Nothing can be more evident than that the chief intent of this parable is to show that the Church of Christ is to be a mixture of good and bad people until the end of the world. It is like a *feast* where both good and bad guests are entertained; but can it be like such a *feast* if only the *invisibly* virtuous are members of it? If the subjects of this kingdom are of only one *invisible* kind, how can they bear any resemblance to a *feast* made up of *all kinds* of guests? In fact, what could be imagined that is more unlike this kingdom, if it were truly such a kingdom as you have represented it?

How could our blessed Savior have more directly guarded against such a description of his kingdom as your Lordship <note>Law is addressing Benjamin Hoadly, the Bishop of Bangor, who argued that the true Church was an invisible society of the sincere.</note> has given us, than he has done in these parables? He compares it to a quantity of good and bad fish in a *net*, and to a number of good and bad guests at a *feast*. Are there any words that could more fully declare his meaning to be that his kingdom consisted of both good and bad subjects? Could anyone more directly contradict this account of our Savior than by saying that his kingdom is an "invisible" kingdom, consisting only of a particular sort of people who are "invisibly virtuous"?

Your Lordship professes a great respect for the Scriptures and a strong dislike for all doctrines that are not found there. There is as much authority from Scripture to prove that the Church is a *kingdom without any subjects* as there is to prove that only those who have such *invisible graces* belong to it. And it is as easy to prove from those sacred *writings* that neither Christ nor his Apostles were ever *visible* on earth as it is to prove that the number of people on earth who believe in Christ constitute the *invisible church.*

I admit that one can easily imagine a group of people whose internal and invisible graces might entitle them to the favor of God. These could be called an *invisible number*, or *congregation*, or *church*, because it is invisible to us where they are or how many of them there are. But then, my Lord, it is a great mistake if this Invisible Church is opposed to, or distinguished from, the *Visible Church* in regards to *external ordinances*. For in these matters, both are *equally* obliged to be *visible*. This is the only *number* of people or *church* to which the *Invisible Church* is actually opposed. For just as the "Invisible Church" refers to a group so named because of their *invisible graces*, this invisibly good Church can only *truly* be opposed to the *invisibly bad church*—that is, those people who are not the same *inwardly* as they profess to be *outwardly*.

For our blessed Lord's statement that his disciples *were not of this world* proves that *St. Peter* and *St. Paul* had no distinct powers from presbyters and deacons just as strictly as his saying that *his kingdom was not of this world* proves that there is no real or necessary difference between bishops and presbyters in his kingdom. <note>The author is attacking the Bishop's argument that a spiritual kingdom should have no earthly hierarchy.</note> And it is as much a logical error to say that because the disciples of Christ were not of this world, there was no necessity for some to have been *apostles* and others *presbyters*, as it is to say that because Christ's kingdom is not of this world, there is no necessity for some to be bishops and others presbyters within it.

I have been especially detailed in examining the text of your sermon and comparing your doctrines closely to it so that every reader who has common sense may be able to perceive that your doctrines relate no more to that text than if you had derived them from the first verse in the first chapter of *Genesis*. <note>The author is mocking the Bishop by suggesting his interpretation of "Christ's kingdom is not of this world" is as irrelevant as the creation story in Genesis would be to this specific argument.</note>

But to go on, you say that all *resistance* is not rebellion, and as proof of it, you say that all *church* separation is not *schism*. This plainly implies that there is *at least* as much difference between some *separations* from *different* churches as there is between some armed *resistances* against *different* kings. This is as rational an argument as if it were said: "Someone killed a man *lawfully* (such as in self-defense or state execution); therefore, anyone else may kill a man *unlawfully*." For if some separation may be a *duty* and some separation a *sin*, it is as false and ridiculous to infer that because *our* separation is just, it justifies *all other* separations, as it would be to conclude that because we may do our *duty*, others may transgress their *duty*. 

For there being manifestly—and by your own acknowledgment—this great difference between one *separation* and another *separation*, one *separation* in such circumstances will no more justify a *separation* in other circumstances than the *lawfulness* of killing a man in some cases will prove it lawful to kill a man in all other cases.

<margin>* Representation, page 4.</margin>
The learned committee <note>The committee of the Lower House of Convocation, which was tasked with examining Hoadly's sermon for "subversive" doctrines.</note> charged your lordship with *denying all authority to the church, and leaving it without any authority to judge, censure, or punish offenders in the affairs of conscience and eternal salvation.* * To support this charge, they quoted these words from your sermon: *Christ is the sole lawgiver to his subjects, and himself the sole judge of their behavior in the affairs of conscience and salvation; in these points he has left behind him no visible human authority.*

## Of the Authority of the Church, as it relates to Excommunication.

In order to justify this doctrine <note>The doctrine of the Church's authority to excommunicate offenders.</note> thoroughly and show the foundation <note>original: "bottom"</note> upon which it is built, I shall, as briefly as I can, state the *nature* and *intent* of spiritual punishments and show what *effects* they have on offenders in the next world. From this, I am convinced it will further appear that such *effects* no more exclude people from the righteous judgment of God than the heathens are excluded from His righteous judgment.

<margin>Page 39.</margin>

I shall therefore, my Lord, ask leave to show that the power of excommunication is a *judicial power*. <meta>This page continues William Law’s argument that excommunication is a formal, judicial act. Having previously asserted that excommunication is more than just social shunning, Law now argues that the authority to exclude people from the Church necessarily rests with the same individuals who have the authority to admit them—namely, the clergy.</meta>

->( 113 )<-
->I<-

The fact that excommunication is a power belonging only to specific individuals will be clear from the nature of the act itself, since it is the exclusion of people from Christian worship. Because only specific men can *preside over* <note>original: "officiate in"</note> Christian worship and admit people into communion, it follows that only those same persons can refuse the Sacrament and exclude offenders from that communion. Nothing can be more plain: those who alone have the right to administer the Sacrament are the only ones who can exclude people from it.

All people are admitted into the Christian covenant on certain conditions. They only have a right to its benefits, or the ordinary "means of grace" <note>Means of grace: the sacraments and spiritual practices through which God's help is believed to be given to believers.</note>, as long as they fulfill the conditions of their admission. Furthermore, the very people who alone have the authority to admit them into the Church based on those conditions also alone have the authority to exclude them if they fail to perform those conditions. 

Their act of exclusion is just as *effective* <note>original: "effectual"</note> at stripping away all the privileges of Christians—and just as truly makes them *strangers* <note>original: "Aliens"</note> to the Kingdom of God—as their initial act of admission entitled them to all the benefits of Church communion. Since they have just as much authority to exclude some as they have to admit others into the Church—the authority being the same in both cases—it must be equally effective in both situations.

<meta>This page continues William Law’s argument that the power of excommunication—the authority to exclude someone from the Church—is not a general right held by all Christians, but a specific authority given to the clergy, just as the power to admit new members through baptism is reserved for them.</meta>

If your Lordship will say that all people are equally qualified to admit persons into the Church—that the command, *Go ye, and baptize all nations*, conferred the same powers on all Christians—then indeed it must be granted that excommunication, or exclusion from the Church, is a right equally invested in all Christians. But as sure as Christ gave specific <note>original: "peculiar"</note> powers to his Apostles, and as sure as they left particular men to succeed them in those powers, so sure is it that only such successors can either admit or exclude persons from Christian communion.

Secondly, that excommunication belongs to particular persons will appear from its institution in Scripture:

> *If your brother shall trespass against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone. But if he will not hear you, then take with you one or two more. Here, my Lord, is as plain an institution of excommunication as can well be conceived.

First, we may observe that an authority is given here to the Church over the offender. This is *such* an authority that did not belong to private men, whether acting separately or united together. This is the description of that Church before whom the offender was to be brought, and whose authority Christ promises to support; it is *two or three met together in his name*.

We will more easily understand what is meant by the *effects* of *spiritual punishments* <note>spiritual punishments: ecclesiastical penalties, such as excommunication or being barred from the sacraments.</note> if we consider them under this division:

Now, as for the primary and intended effects of spiritual punishments, they are these:

<margin>* Ephesians 5:27</margin>
First, to preserve the honor of God and his Church, so that by removing corrupt members, the Church might be presented as a glorious Church, *not having spot or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it might be holy and without blemish* <note>original: "not having Spot or Wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it might be Holy, and without Blemish"; Ephesians 5:27.</note>.

Secondly, to reform offenders and reclaim them from their vices; it is a discipline given to the Church for the edification <note>edification: the spiritual or moral instruction and improvement of a person.</note>, and not the destruction, of its members.
