If it is a mere trifle—altogether insignificant to us regarding God's favor—to be expelled from the Church by such an authority, then it must be just as much of a *trifle* to be admitted into the Church by that same authority.

Therefore, whoever declares the one also plainly declares the other. It is perfectly clear: if nothing is *lost* regarding God's favor when we are properly expelled from the Church, then nothing is *gained* regarding God's favor when we are properly admitted into the Church.

For if being a member of the Church were any step toward God's favor, or made us more acceptable to Him, then those degrees of favor and acceptance must certainly be lost when we lose the very thing that caused them.

<meta>This page continues William Law’s argument that being a Christian is inseparable from "external communion" (participation in the visible Church). He responds to Bishop Hoadly's view that church membership is a matter of individual conscience rather than divine requirement.</meta>

( 161 )

<meta>The text continues the argument that a person's status as a Christian is tied to their outward participation in the church: "...cannot be taken, in] general, as he who is not in outward communion, for a Christian."</note>

The Christian religion is a method of worship distinct from all others in those offices and duties which constitute *outward communion* <note>original: "external Communion"; the act of participating in the public services, sacraments, and visible community of the Church</note>. Therefore, if you are obligated to be a Christian—meaning you must serve God differently from other people—you are obligated to *outward communion*. This is because the service which distinguishes the Christian worshipper from all other people is the kind of service that can only be performed in an outward communion through specific acts: namely, *professions of faith*, *joint prayers*, and the *observance of the sacraments*. 

*Outward communion* is simply another word for the profession of Christianity. The various duties and obligations that concern a person as a Christian and distinguish them from others are duties that necessarily imply *outward communion*, just as *walking* implies *motion*. Therefore, to ask whether a Christian is obligated to outward communion is like asking whether a person who is obligated to walk is obligated to move. 

The short of it is this: no one can be a Christian except by taking upon themselves the profession of Christianity. The profession of Christianity is nothing else but outward communion with Christians. Therefore, it is as necessary to be in outward communion as it is to be a Christian.

I hope I do not need to prove to your Lordship <note>Bishop Benjamin Hoadly, the Bishop of Bangor, whose sermon sparked this controversy</note> that there is an *authority* to oblige people to—

...the profession of Christianity; I intend here only to prove that the same *authority* obliges us to *outward communion* <note>original: "external Communion"; the act of participating in the public services, sacraments, and visible community of the Church</note>.

Therefore, if your **Lordship** <note>Law is addressing Benjamin Hoadly, the Bishop of Bangor</note> had declared to the world that you know of no *authority* to oblige *people* to be *Christians*, it would have been just as *innocent* and *true* a declaration as this one you have made concerning *outward communion*. For, my **Lord**, what is implied in *outward communion* other than our communicating with our *fellow Christians* in those acts of worship and *divine service* which *Christianity* requires of us? So, if we prove ourselves to be *Christians*, we must prove ourselves to be in this *outward communion*. This is because to be a *Christian* implies nothing more than being among the number of those who visibly unite and join in such acts and offices of *divine worship* as are appropriate for *Christians*. If, therefore, there is *no authority* to oblige us to *outward communion*, then no one is obliged to be a *Christian*.

Therefore, this authority—which began with the existence of the Church and flowed from the very *nature* of the Church—may very justly be called *church authority*.

If it should be asked whether this *authority* is absolute, I answer: it is just as absolute as that *authority* which obliges us to be baptized. Our *Saviour* has told us that if *we are not baptized, we shall be damned.* Here, therefore, is an *authority* for *baptism*. The Scripture has not said whether this is so absolutely obliging that there is no room in any case for a *dispensation* <note>original: "Dispensation"; a divinely granted exemption from a rule or requirement.</note>; therefore, it is not a case that concerns us. Now the *authority* which obliges us to *external communion* <note>original: "external Communion"; visible participation in the communal life, rituals, and sacraments of the organized Church.</note> is based on the *same terms*. The thing is as plainly required as *baptism*; but whether it will be dispensed with in any specific cases is something we have nothing to do with. If there is any *sincerity*, any *weakness*, any *ignorance*, or the *lack* of anything that would excuse those who refuse to be baptized, those same considerations may excuse the *refusal* of *external communion* with the *church*.

This, my Lord, is the *nature* of that *church authority* which obliges us to *external communion*. It is that very *same authority* which obliges us to the *profession* of *Christianity* or to enter into a *covenant* <note>original: "Covenant"; a formal, divinely sanctioned agreement between God and His people, often established through religious rites.</note> with *God*. From what has been said on this subject, the following propositions are clearly true:

First: Because joining any particular part of the Church implies our joining the Church of Christ—or, in other words, our embracing Christianity—it follows clearly that the *same* authority which requires us to embrace *Christianity* also requires us to enter into that sound *part* of Christ’s Church where we live.

Secondly: This authority does not arise from any *human laws* or the power which any men, in whatever position they may be, have over others. Rather, it is the authority of God, who has established this Church in order to require all mankind to enter into it.

Thirdly: This authority from God may be very properly called *church authority*, because God demonstrated this authority to the world by the *establishment* <note>original: "institution"</note> of the Church. ...because it is *established*, any more than we ought to leave our Church if it were *persecuted*. <note>original: "established"; this refers to the Church of England being the official state religion by law.</note>

The short of it is this:
The *Church Authority* which obliges us to external communion <note>original: "communion"; participation in the life, sacraments, and worship of a specific church body.</note> with any *particular* part of Christ's Church is that *same divine authority* which calls upon us to be *baptized* and to enter into a covenant with God.

Now, if *human laws*—whether of the *church* or the *state*—align with this authority, then they oblige us just as they do in other cases where they require us to do what the *laws* of *God* already required. But if *human laws*, whether of the *church* or the *state*, require us to enter into *such a communion* that does not have the *authority* of Christ behind it, or if they forbid us from joining *such a communion* as is a *true part* of Christ's Church, such laws are no more to be observed than if they had established *idolatry* or forbidden the worship of the true God.

For *human laws* are not supposed to create our *duty* to enter into *such a communion*; rather, they are applied as proper *means* to induce us to do what the *laws* of *God* had already made our *duty* to do. And it is undeniably true that, though there should be ever so many *human laws* commanding us to enter into any particular communion, we must not comply with such laws unless they concern *such a communion* as it was our *duty* to enter into, even if no *such human laws* were in existence.

<summary>Law argues that human laws (state or church) only have power when they align with divine mandates; we are bound to a church by God's authority, not by the government's establishment of it.</summary>

So that *human* Laws create no *necessity* of external *communion* <note>original: "external communion"; the act of participating in the public worship and sacraments of a specific church body.</note>, any more than they create the *necessity* of praying to God. The question, therefore, in any *country* is not this: whether the laws of either their *church* or *state* require us to enter into *such* a communion. Instead, the question is whether it is *such* a communion as it would be our *duty* to enter into even if there were no *human* laws to mandate it—whether it be a *part* of Christ’s Church which we are obligated to enter into on pain of everlasting damnation.

When, therefore, you say that if the people of *England* are obligated by a *human* authority, as *such*, to enter into the Church of *England*, then the people of *France*, *Spain*, and *Italy* are just as truly obligated by the human authority there to enter into those particular communions—you speak the absolute truth. *First*: That by entering into any *particular communion*, we are to understand the same thing as entering into the *Church of Christ*, or embracing the *religion* which *Christ* has established.

Here lies the *great fallacy* in this argument: you use the same word (namely <note>original: "viz."</note> *justified*) in relation to both these groups of people in the very *same sense*. <sig>P</sig>

For as religion in general is *good*, because it does us *good* and brings us into *favor* with God; so the particular *excellence* and *goodness* of any religion must consist in this: that it does us a *more particular good* and raises us to *higher degrees* of *God's favor* than a *less excellent* religion would have done.

So that when your Lordship <note>Referring to Benjamin Hoadly, the Bishop of Bangor, to whom this letter is addressed.</note> talks of the *excellence* of one religion above another as having nothing in it, as *such*, to recommend us to higher degrees of God's favor or to achieve our *justification* <note>original: "effect our Justification"; the process by which a person is deemed righteous before God.</note>; it is fully as absurd as to say that though one kind of *learning* may be more *excellent* than another kind of *learning*, yet no men are more *excellent* or valuable for having one kind of *learning* than another.

For just as no kind of *learning* can be said to be uniquely *excellent* unless it gives some unique *excellence* to those who are *masters* of it; so no kind of *religion* can be said to be *more excellent* than another, unless those who profess it reap some *advantage* from it which is not to be had from a *religion less excellent*.

From all this, it appears, first, that there can be no such thing as any *goodness* or *excellence* in one religion above another, except as it procures a specific *good* and *advantage* to those who profess it.

Secondly, your Lordship can allow no other *goodness* or *excellence* in *religion*—even based on your own express *words*—except that which implies as great an *absurdity* as to allow for good *food*, good *learning*, or good *advice* which can do nobody any good *at all*.

So, whether you will yet admit that you have destroyed all the difference between *religions* or not, I cannot tell; yet I imagine everyone will see that you have only left such a *goodness* in one *religion* over another as can do nobody any good *at all*. 

The point is this: If you will admit there is no *excellence* in one *religion* over another, then you are guilty of making *Christianity* no better than *Islam* <note>original: "Mahometanism"; an archaic term for the religion of Islam.</note>. But if you will acknowledge a *goodness* and *excellence* in one *religion* over another and yet contend that it is *sincerity alone* which does us *any good* or recommends us to the *favor* of *God* in all *religions* alike, this is as absurd as to say such a thing is *much better* for us than any other thing, while also asserting that *any other thing* will do us *as much good* as *that*.

# Regarding the Reformation

I will proceed now, in a word or two, to show that the *necessity* of *communion* <note>original: "Communion"; the act of participating in the shared worship and sacraments of a church.</note> with any *particular* church, and the *effects* of *excommunication* <note>original: "Excommunication"; a formal censure that excludes a person from the sacraments and membership of the church.</note>, are perfectly consistent with the principles of the Reformation.

<margin>Answer to the Representation, page 118.</margin>

> You say, *If there is a church authority to oblige people to external communion—I beg to know how the Reformation itself can be justified. For there was at that time an order of churchmen, vested with all spiritual authority—there was, therefore, a church authority to oblige Christians, a power of some over others. To what, therefore, do we owe this very Church of England?*

To this, it may be answered:

First, that this argument proceeds upon a false supposition—namely, that it is the *laws of any men* which oblige us to external communion. I have already shown this to be as false as the idea that it is the *laws of any men* which oblige us to be Christians.

<summary>The author begins a defense of the Church of England's authority, arguing that the Reformation was not a rejection of church authority itself, but a realignment with divine requirements rather than human laws.</summary>
<keywords>Reformation, Church Authority, Communion, Excommunication, Church of England, Bangorian Controversy, spiritual authority</keywords>

--- Page 370 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's argument from page 215, further justifying the Reformation by explaining that religious obligation stems from divine institution rather than human law.</meta>

( 216 )

Secondly: That there may be a *real* and a great *authority* which obliges us to *external communion* <note>original: "external Communion"; the visible practice of participating in public worship and the sacraments.</note>, even though this authority is not founded in any *human laws*. For there is as real and apparent an authority for *baptism*, the *Supper* of the *Lord*, and other parts of external communion as if they were the express subject of any *human laws*.

Thirdly: That the *laws* of *men* in this *affair* of *religion* carry the *same obligation* and *force* that they do in other *matters*. If they command "indifferent" things <note>original: "Things indifferent"; religious practices or rites not explicitly commanded or forbidden by the Bible, which are left to the discretion of church or state leaders.</note>, they are to be obeyed out of respect for the authority of the command. If they enjoin things that are inherently good by their own nature, the necessity of obedience is greater. But if they command things that are unlawful, we are not to comply, but must obey *God* rather than *man*.

Fourthly: The *question* therefore at the *Reformation* was not whether the *laws* of the *Pope* or the *Prince* were on the side of the *Church* of *Rome*, but whether that *faith* and those *institutions* which constitute the *Christian religion* were with the *Reformers* or with the Roman Catholics <note>original: "Papists"; a term used in this period for those loyal to the Pope.</note>. The necessity of being in external communion <note>original: "external Communion"; the visible practice of participating in public worship and the sacraments.</note> does not obligate us to be in communion with the Pope or any number of bishops *simply because of their titles*, whose authority we might happen to be born under. Instead, it obligates us to be in that communion which follows the *way* or *method* of salvation that Christ has *instituted* <note>original: "instituted"; formally established or set up as a religious practice.</note>.

So, even if we were to grant that during the Reformation we broke the *human* laws of the *church* which required us to remain in communion with the Church of *Rome*, it by no means follows that we violated *that authority* which obligates us to external communion. This is because *that authority* is not based on any *human laws*, but is the authority of Christ, requiring us to observe everything that constitutes external communion. For just as it is the authority of Christ that obliges us to be *Christians*, that same authority obliges us to enter into that communion where the *institutions* and faith of Christ are preserved.

Here, let common sense judge whether this argument of yours—which attempts to show the unreasonableness of claiming any significance in *excommunication* <note>exclusion from the church community and its rituals</note> simply because we disregarded the excommunication of the Church of Rome—does not also prove it equally unreasonable to insist upon the *necessity* of any *faith*, or any *sacraments*, or any *canonical books* <note>the books of the Bible officially accepted as genuine and inspired</note>, just because we denied the <term>Romish</term> <note>original: "Romish"; a term used historically by Protestants to refer to the Roman Catholic Church</note> creed, the Roman Catholic sacraments, and their <term>canon of scripture</term>?

For our <term>Reformers</term> <note>leaders of the Protestant Reformation who sought to change the church's practices</note> no more intended to show that excommunication was a *dream* or a *trifle* <note>a thing of little value or importance</note> by disregarding the excommunication of the Church of Rome, than they intended to show that all *sacraments*, all *faith*, and all *scripture* were *dreams* and *trifles* by not accepting the sacraments, the creed, or the canon of the Church of Rome. 

And, my Lord, what a "worthy" defender of *Christianity* and the Reformation would he be who should ask us what we mean by the necessity of sacraments, or faith, or scripture, since we have not allowed the necessity of the Roman Catholic sacraments, faith, or scripture? Yet, such a *defender* is your Lordship, who...

<sig>Q 2</sig>

[The Bishop] contends that we ought to reject excommunication as a *trifle* and a *dream* because we disregarded the excommunication of the Church of *Rome*.

I have now gone as far in the examination of your *doctrines* as my present purpose will allow me. I am inclined to think that in this and my former *letters*, I have gone far enough to show that a few more *such defenses of Christianity and the Reformation* as you have given us would complete their ruin, as far as *human writings* can complete it.

Even if you had intended to cause a great deal of harm to *Christianity* and the *Reformation*, I believe no one who wishes for their confusion would have thought you could have taken a better way to achieve that end than by writing as you have lately written.

For anyone who would not think it sufficient to place *Christianity* and *Mahometanism* <note>original: "Mahometanism"; an archaic and often derogatory term for Islam</note>, or the *Reformation* and *Quakerism* <note>the beliefs of the Religious Society of Friends; at the time, this was seen by the established Church as a radical or informal version of Christianity</note> on the same footing, must be a very *bitter enemy* to them both.

And anyone would have to be very slow to understand if they do not see that this is plainly done by reducing everything to *private persuasion* and making *sincerity* in every religion—whether true or false—the same claim to the same degrees of God’s favor.

<meta>This page begins the postscript to William Law's letter to the Bishop of Bangor, responding to the Bishop's controversial views on "sincerity" and "erroneous conscience." Law is refining his argument about how God judges those who are sincere but mistaken in their religious beliefs.</meta>

# POSTSCRIPT.

The Learned Committee observed to your Lordship that *an erroneous conscience was never, until now, allowed to wholly justify men in their errors.* <note>The "Learned Committee" refers to the Lower House of Convocation, which formally investigated the Bishop of Bangor’s sermon for perceived heterodoxy.</note>

I have shown this observation to be *true* and *just*, as it implies that although sincerity in an *erroneous* <note>original: "erroneous"; here referring to religious practices that Law considers outside the established, true Church.</note> way of worship might, to some degree or another, recommend men to the favor or mercy of God, it is not the same *entire* recommendation to his favor that is achieved by our sincere obedience in the *true way of salvation*. That is, although it might justify them in *some* degree, it cannot justify them to the same *extent* as those who sincerely serve God in the true religion that he himself has established.

Now, our justification <note>original: "Justification"; the theological term for being declared righteous or "just" in the eyes of God.</note>, as it is brought about by the merits of Christ, is always to *one and the same* degree. However, as our justification is influenced by our own behavior, it is as capable of *different degrees* as our virtue and holiness are capable of *different degrees*. It is also necessary that our justification be *greater* or *lesser*, according to whether our holiness is *greater* or *lesser*.

<summary>William Law argues that while sincerity in a mistaken faith might earn some of God's mercy, it does not equal the full justification granted to those who sincerely follow the true, divinely established religion.</summary>

<keywords>William Law, justification, sincerity, erroneous conscience, holiness, salvation, Bangorian Controversy, merits of Christ</keywords>

<meta>This page continues William Law’s postscript, specifically addressing the Bishop of Bangor’s claim that "sincerity" must either justify a person entirely or not at all. Yet in answer to this observation of the Learned Committee, you say, *it must either justify them, or not justify them; it must either justify them wholly, or not justify them at all.* This, my Lord, is as contrary to the Scripture as it is to the observation of the Committee. For our blessed Savior, speaking of the *Publican* <note>original: "Publican"; a tax collector, typically viewed as a sinner in the New Testament context.</note>, says, *I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other* <margin>Luke 18:10, etc.</margin>.

Here, my Lord, is as plain a declaration of *degrees* in justification as can well be made, so far as justification can be effected by our own behavior.

For, it is plain, the *Publican* was not wholly justified, because then there would be no need for him to embrace Christianity; it is also plain that he was justified *in part*, or else he could not be said to be justified *rather than the Pharisee* <note>original: "Pharisee"; a member of a Jewish sect known for strict adherence to the law, often depicted as self-righteous.</note>.

If therefore your answer refutes the observation of the Learned Committee, it must also refute this passage of Scripture.

I shall only add one word in relation to another point.

I have already shown the falseness and evil tendency of your argument against *excommunication* <note>original: "Excommunication"; the formal exclusion of a member from the sacraments and fellowship of the Church.</note>, which you asserted to be a *dream and trifle without any effect*, because it is our *own behavior* alone which can signify—

As in these examples:

> *Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins* \*;
> *In whom we have redemption through his blood* †;

It is the constant, uniform doctrine of Scripture that our reconciliation and peace with God, and our justification and sanctification <note>The process of being made holy.</note> before God, are owing to the *merits and death of Christ*. But if what you have said is true—that it is our *behavior alone* which procures the favor of God—then the *blood* of Christ must be as truly without any effect as excommunication is without any effect.

**Christian Morals and Christian Prudence** in two parts. In which is shown the unique wisdom and beauty of the Christian religion, in its general design of promoting those two excellent ends so perfecting to human nature: purity and peace. By John Lawrence, Master of Arts, Rector of Yelvertoft in Northamptonshire. Octavo, 1717.

**Sermons and Discourses** on several subjects and occasions. By Robert South, Doctor of Divinity, late Prebendary of Westminster, and Canon of Christ-Church, Oxford <note>original: "Oxon"</note>, etc. In six volumes, Octavo, 1717.

**Sermons on Several Occasions**. By Dr. Sharp, late Lord Archbishop of York. In four volumes, Octavo. The fourth edition, 1717.

**The Old and New Testament Connected** in the history of the Jews and neighboring nations, from the decline <note>original: "Declension"</note> of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah to the times of Christ. By Humphrey Prideaux, Doctor of Divinity. Two volumes Folio, or three volumes Octavo.

**The Christian’s Pattern**: Or, a Treatise on the Imitation of Jesus Christ. In four books. Written originally in Latin by Thomas à Kempis. Now rendered into English, to which are added meditations and prayers for sick persons, by George Stanhope, Doctor of Divinity, Dean of Canterbury. The ninth edition, Octavo, 1717.

**Rapin on Gardens**: A Latin poem. In four books. Translated into English <note>original: "Englished"</note> by Mr. Gardiner. The second edition, Octavo, 1719.

**A Paraphrase** with short and useful notes on the books of the Old Testament. Part I, in two volumes, containing the five books of Moses. With a complete index of the principal matters, words, and phrases in the said books. For the use of families. By Thomas Pyle, Master of Arts, Lecturer of King's Lynn <note>original: "Lynn-Regis"</note> in Norfolk. Octavo, 1717.

**The Practice of Divine Love Revised**: Being an exposition of the Church Catechism. By the Right Reverend Father in God, Thomas Ken <note>original: "Kenn"</note>, Doctor of Divinity, late Bishop of Bath and Wells. To which are added directions for prayer. Octavo, 1718.

**A Companion for the Festivals and Fasts of the Church of England**, with short prayers <note>original: "Collects"</note> and prayers for each solemnity. By Robert Nelson, Esq. The tenth edition, Octavo, 1717.
